name: Icelandic Commonwealth (930-1262 AD)
description: Founded in 930 by Norse settlers, the Commonwealth was a unique political experiment without a king. Governance relied on the Althing, where 'Goðar' (chiefs) legislated and settled disputes. This era saw the settlement of the island and the later adoption of Christianity in 1000. However, internal power struggles during the Age of the Sturlungs weakened the social fabric. In 1262, the Old Covenant was signed, ending Icelandic sovereignty and placing the nation under the Norwegian Crown, marking the start of centuries of foreign rule.

name: Iceland (1918-present)
description: Iceland regained sovereignty in 1918 as a kingdom in personal union with Denmark. During WWII, after Denmark’s fall, the island was strategically occupied by British and later U.S. forces to secure the Atlantic. This period accelerated the move to full independence, leading to the foundation of a Republic in 1944. Since then, Iceland has transformed from a poor fishing society into a prosperous democracy, navigating the Cold War, the Cod Wars with Britain, and the 2008 financial crisis while preserving its ancient Althing traditions.

name: Ireland 1922–Present
description: Ireland emerged as an independent state in 1922 after the Anglo-Irish Treaty ended the Irish War of Independence against the United Kingdom. The island was partitioned, with Northern Ireland remaining part of the UK while the rest became the Irish Free State. In 1937 a new constitution established the modern state, later declared a republic in 1949. Since then its borders have remained stable. Ireland has developed into a modern European democracy known for its cultural heritage, economic growth, and strong role in the European Union.

name: Kingdom of Ulaid (400–1177 AD)
description: Ulaid was an early Gaelic kingdom located in the northeastern part of Ireland, roughly corresponding to parts of modern Ulster. Its origins lie in ancient tribal societies recorded in Irish mythology and early medieval chronicles. The kingdom was associated with the legendary capital of Emain Macha and figures from the Ulster Cycle such as Cú Chulainn. Over centuries its territory shrank as rival dynasties expanded. In 1177 the Norman invasion of Ireland led to the collapse of Ulaid’s political power and the region was reorganized under Norman rule.

name: Kingdom of Airgíalla (330–735 AD)
description: Airgíalla was a federation of several Gaelic kingdoms located in what is now central and northern Ireland, mainly across modern counties Armagh, Monaghan, and parts of Tyrone and Louth. According to medieval tradition it was founded by the Three Collas around the 4th or 5th century after defeating the Ulaid and seizing territory from them. Rather than a single centralized state, Airgíalla functioned as a loose alliance of ruling dynasties. Its autonomy gradually declined with the expansion of neighboring powers and later English influence in Ireland.

name: Kingdom of Ailech (450–1185 AD)
description: The Kingdom of Ailech was a powerful Gaelic kingdom in northwestern Ireland associated with the Cenél nEógain dynasty of the Northern Uí Néill. Centered on the royal site of Grianan of Ailech in present-day County Donegal, it emerged during the early medieval period and became one of the dominant powers in Ulster. Its rulers often contested the High Kingship of Ireland and influenced regional politics for centuries. In the late 12th century the Anglo-Norman invasion of Ireland weakened the traditional Gaelic order, and by 1185 the kingdom effectively collapsed, giving way to later Gaelic lordships.

name: Kingdom of Connacht (400–1226 AD)
description: Connacht was one of the principal Gaelic kingdoms of western Ireland, traditionally ruled by the Uí Briúin dynasty and later dominated by the O'Connor kings. Its early royal center was at Cruachan, an important political and mythological site in Irish tradition. Throughout the medieval period Connacht was a major regional power and its rulers occasionally claimed the High Kingship of Ireland. After the Anglo-Norman invasion in the late 12th century, Norman lords gradually seized territory. By 1226 the kingdom experienced significant territorial changes as Norman control expanded across parts of the province.

name: Kingdom of Mide (400–1172 AD)
description: The Kingdom of Mide was a major Gaelic kingdom located in central Ireland, roughly corresponding to the modern region of Meath and surrounding areas. It was closely associated with the Southern Uí Néill dynasty, whose rulers often held the High Kingship of Ireland. The royal hill of Uisneach served as an important ceremonial and symbolic center of the island. Mide played a key political role during the early medieval period, but its power declined after the Anglo-Norman invasion of Ireland, when much of its territory was reorganized under Norman lordship.

name: Norse Kingdom of Dublin (841–1171 AD)
description: The Norse Kingdom of Dublin was founded in 841 when Viking raiders established a permanent longphort, or fortified ship camp, at the site of present-day Dublin. It soon developed into a powerful Hiberno-Norse city-state controlling important trade routes across the Irish Sea. The settlement became a major center for commerce, slavery, and Viking naval activity, linking Ireland with Scandinavia and Britain. Over time the Norse rulers adopted Christianity and interacted closely with Gaelic kingdoms. The kingdom ended in 1171 when Anglo-Norman forces captured Dublin during the Norman invasion of Ireland.

name: Kingdom of Mumhain (400–859 AD)
description: The Kingdom of Mumhain, known in English as Munster, was one of the great overkingdoms of early medieval Ireland. Emerging from earlier tribal confederations, it was dominated by the powerful Eóganachta dynasties and ruled much of southern Ireland from the royal site of Cashel. The kingdom played an important role in Irish politics, religion, and culture during the early medieval period. In the 9th century internal divisions and regional rivalries reshaped the province. Around 859 the territory of Osraighe was politically separated from Munster’s direct control, marking a significant territorial change.

name: Kingdom of Mumhain (969–1117 AD)
currency: Barter economy and Hiberno-Norse silver coinage in coastal trade
description: The Kingdom of Mumhain, or Munster, remained one of the major Gaelic overkingdoms of southern Ireland during the late early medieval period. In 969 the Munster forces reconquered Luimneach (Limerick), a Norse coastal settlement that had developed into an important Viking trading center. Although Gaelic kings ruled most of the interior, several Norse city-states continued to exist along the coasts, maintaining trade networks across the Irish Sea. During this period Munster rose to great power under the Dál gCais dynasty. In 1117 the kingdom was formally divided into the separate kingdoms of Thomond and Desmond.

name: Kingdom of Osraighe (859–1171 AD)
description: The Kingdom of Osraighe was a Gaelic kingdom located in southeastern Ireland, roughly corresponding to modern County Kilkenny and parts of Laois. Although its ruling dynasty was ancient, the kingdom became politically distinct from Munster around 859 when regional power shifts reduced Munster’s authority over the area. Ruled mainly by the Mac Giolla Phádraig dynasty, Osraighe held a strategic position between the larger kingdoms of Munster and Leinster. Its rulers frequently shifted alliances to preserve autonomy until the Anglo-Norman invasion brought the region under Norman control.

name: Norse Settlement of Cork (848–1174 AD)
currency: Hiberno-Norse silver coinage and trade by weight
description: The Norse settlement of Cork emerged during the Viking Age as Scandinavian traders and raiders established a coastal base along the River Lee. Founded in the early 10th century, it functioned as a small Hiberno-Norse trading town connected to wider Viking networks across the Irish Sea and the North Atlantic. Unlike larger Viking cities such as Dublin or Limerick, Cork remained a more modest settlement but still played a role in maritime trade and regional politics. The Norse presence declined after the Anglo-Norman invasion of Ireland in the late 12th century.

name: Kingdom of Leinster (841–1171 AD)
currency: Barter economy and Hiberno-Norse silver coinage in coastal trade
description: The Kingdom of Leinster was a major Gaelic kingdom in eastern Ireland. In 841 Viking settlers established fortified bases at Dubh Linn (Dublin) and Veisafjǫrðr (Wexford), seizing important coastal territory and creating Norse trading towns linked to the wider Irish Sea network. Despite losing these ports, Leinster remained an influential regional power ruled mainly by the Uí Dúnlainge and later the Uí Cheinnselaig dynasties. The kingdom continued to compete with neighboring Irish rulers until 1171, when the Anglo-Norman invasion ended Leinster’s sovereignty and brought the region under Norman control.

name: Norse Settlement of Wexford (841–1169 AD)
currency: Hiberno-Norse silver coinage and trade by weight
description: Veisafjǫrðr was a Norse coastal settlement established by Viking groups in 841 on the southeastern coast of Ireland at the site of modern Wexford. It developed as a Hiberno-Norse port linked to maritime trade routes across the Irish Sea and the wider Viking world. The town served as a base for commerce, ship activity, and regional influence while coexisting with nearby Gaelic kingdoms such as Leinster. Over time Norse settlers integrated with local Irish society and adopted Christianity. The settlement lost its independence in 1169 when Anglo-Norman forces landed at Wexford during the Norman invasion of Ireland.

name: High Kingship of Ireland (1002–1014 AD)
currency: Barter economy and Hiberno-Norse silver coinage in trade
description: Between 1002 and 1014 Ireland came closest to political unification under Brian Boru, the High King of Ireland. Originally king of Munster, Brian expanded his power across the island and forced many regional rulers to acknowledge his overlordship. Unlike a centralized kingdom, Ireland remained a network of Gaelic kingdoms whose kings recognized the authority of the High King while retaining local control. Brian also challenged the power of Norse coastal cities such as Dublin. His rule ended in 1014 after the Battle of Clontarf, where his forces won but he was killed.

name: Kingdom of Ireland (1603–1801 AD)
GovernmentType: Constitutional monarchy under the English, later British Crown
description: The Kingdom of Ireland was established in 1542 when the English Crown elevated the former Lordship of Ireland into a kingdom ruled by the English monarch. For much of the 16th century English authority remained limited, as many Gaelic lords retained autonomy. Following the Nine Years’ War and the submission of the last major Gaelic rulers, the crown consolidated control across the island by 1603. Ireland remained a separate kingdom with its own parliament in Dublin. In 1801 the Irish Parliament was dissolved through the Acts of Union, and the kingdom was formally united with Great Britain to create the United Kingdom.
